[an image]
# The New Age May Dawn Suddenly

I just put a movie my father made in 1988 up on the Internet for the first time: [*Where's Utopia?*](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/wheres-utopia-click-read-more-my) It was the result of years of work, traveling to all kinds of communes and communal experiments around the country, trying to answer a question that for him was primary: How do we live together without recreating the same loneliness, domination, and stupidity we were supposedly escaping?

He had already spent 17 years in the [Bruderhof](https://www.bruderhof.com/), a Christian community that doesn’t use money internally. He had no personal money there: income went into the common purse and the community provided what members needed. So when I talk later about moving beyond internal money, I’m not proposing something nobody has ever lived. My father spent most of two decades doing it. They also accepted him as a Jewish atheist, making him a remarkably long-running doctrinal exception. In meditation there, he came to his own understanding that “God is the Universe, and the Universe is Love.”

[an image]
[caption] This was the banner my mom painted that hung in our living room for decades. I will try to locate the actual photo.

He might have stayed, but the U.S. antiwar movement during Vietnam needed somebody who knew how to set up printing presses. He eventually founded the Aquarian Research Foundation—not a commune, but a nonprofit devoted to researching how the planet could have a positive future and publishing what it found. His conclusion was simple and enormous: human beings need small tribal communities again, because [Civilization Is A Hoax,](https://government-scam.blogspot.com/2020/06/everything-you-were-taught-is-lie.html) as I blogged about at the beginning of the Covid plandemic.

That’s where the ***escuelita*** in my title comes in. *Escuelita* means “little school.” I’m borrowing the word from the Zapatistas in Mexico, whose [*Escuelita*](https://schoolsforchiapas.org/advances/schools/la-escuelita/) brought outsiders into their communities for a while to learn autonomy by living it. In the same way, people would live in the healing communities I’m proposing, to heal and to learn the relational and practical methods, so that some of them could eventually leave and set up another one somewhere else. Otherwise, we’ve built a lovely refuge for whoever got there first.

[Share](%%share_url%%)

[image 3]

["Where's Utopia?" (Click READ MORE): My father's 1988 documentary on Communal Living in USA, online for first time ever!](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/wheres-utopia-click-read-more-my)Copy link

I spent much of my childhood being carried through [Twin Oaks](https://twinoaks.org/), [Acorn](https://www.ic.org/directory/acorn-community-farm/), [East Wind](http://eastwind.org/), [Padanaram](https://www.facebook.com/p/Padanaram-100064853281734/), [Zendik](https://highlandscurrent.org/2017/05/09/leaving-zendik-farm/), and many other communities. I was usually just a visitor’s kid, close enough to see how people lived but never quite part of the tribe. At the time that meant a lot of boredom, with some adventures mixed in, but those years gave me a great sample to compare against.

From 1999 to 2001, my family actually lived with the [Love Israel family](https://uwapress.uw.edu/book/9780295988856/the-love-israel-family/) in Washington while escaping [Y2K](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Year_2000_problem), that brief historical period when otherwise reasonable adults prepared for civilization to be defeated by a two-digit date. We lived in a yurt. There were wild berries of every kind, and I loved being in nature. I was also lonely, bored, irritated by the cult programming, and missing my friends in Philadelphia.

I wanted to befriend the children there, but they treated me as an outsider. My mom never liked the place. The leader was also named Love Israel, and to me he seemed like the fakest person I’d ever met, complete with the expected God complex.

We spent a lot of time on our knees in the community garden growing food they could sell in town. The money was opaque and seemed to travel mostly upward toward Love. Meanwhile everybody sang, “Here in the garden, there’s nothing left to do but eat sleep and keep clean.” Again and again. 🌱

My father eventually gave the community his airplane. They sold it instead of using it. He felt tricked, began exposing what was happening, and then we were asked to leave.

The [East Wind](http://eastwind.org/) commune was almost the opposite way. There were maybe eighty people when I was there, enough to have a variety of personalities, small enough to actually make friends. I was happy there. I especially liked showering in a communal shower with both sexes present. I wonder if that still goes on at East Wind? It's the sort of thing that doesn't make it into the history books.

Even at East Wind, though, there was a quieter power issue. They had a nut butter factory that brought in a lot of their income, which seemed to make the woman running it very hard to question. Otherwise I thought the community had a great social life, a nice way of distributing labor, and no obvious guru.

There were like eight people at [Acorn](https://www.ic.org/directory/acorn-community-farm/) when I was there, and no kids. I couldn't tell whether it was a commune I might join or a group of people who were already friends, and who happened to live on some really beautiful land and be good at building cool stuff. Joining would have felt less like applying to a commune than asking whether their group chat had an opening.

[Twin Oaks](https://twinoaks.org/) was much bigger, like two or three hundred people at the time, and almost institutional. It was friendly and interesting, but I didn't feel like I was in a tribe there. It was more like a tiny hippie town, but with a highly structured political system that didn't seem intuitive for hippies.

Looking back, almost none of these communities had a communal therapy practice. People brought the usual human pain and suffering with them, and it all got translated into politics.

Which meant weekly meetings, run according to Robert's Rules of Order, with enormous agendas, where most of the things you needed to talk about couldn't be talked about, and you generally felt like you'd rather be sleeping. (Some people, including me, solved this problem by just going to sleep in the meeting and openly snoring.)

[Zendik](https://highlandscurrent.org/2017/05/09/leaving-zendik-farm/) went in the other direction. They held a brutal community meeting that I’m still recovering from 35 years later. 🤣 Five-year-old me was put in the center and told I was bad because I hadn’t volunteered to help adults with whatever jobs they were doing. Apparently kindergarten had already failed to teach me labor consciousness.

The secular communities often buried hurt under procedure. The spiritual communities often put one person in charge of everybody’s inner life. Most of the rest of this article is my attempt to describe the missing third option.

[Subscribe now](%%checkout_url%%)



# Communes Are Hot Again 🔥

Suddenly the longing behind my father’s movie is everywhere again, and in 2023 [the U.S. Surgeon General](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf) even put out an advisory about it. Or about the loneliness under it, at least. The advisory said roughly half of American adults experience loneliness, and it treated social connection as a public-health issue.

Whether you want to call that loneliness an official “epidemic” or not, it’s obvious that a lot of people can’t tolerate modern life in isolation anymore. They may disagree about politics, food, God, sex, or whether shoes are oppressive, but they agree that something about the current arrangement is starvin’ them.

Check out the Google Trends for “[ecovillage](https://trends.google.com/explore?q=ecovillage&date=all&geo=Worldwide)” and “[intentional community](https://trends.google.com/explore?q=intentional%20community&date=all&geo=Worldwide)”. After years of decline, interest climbed sharply in the mid-2020s.

[an image]
I have no proof that the rise of AI caused this turn, but it’s hard to ignore the coincidence in timing. AI became serious around this time, and it started changing people’s jobs and relationships, and how they see the future. Suddenly, forming a village sounded like a good backup plan, not just a hippie utopian whim.

It’s poppin’ on Instagram too! 🔥 Chantress Seba—my favorite light-language love influencer—[posted an application](https://instagram.com/p/DVyl1a2lAuZ/) for people interested in starting a commune. I applied, although I don’t think she’s coming to Africa, where I'm at. When I saw the post, many thousands of people appeared to be interested. Imagine opening your inbox after casually inviting a million followers to co-found a village.

Later, when another influencer with a big following [floated the commune idea](https://instagram.com/p/DaLvZV2qIk2/), the comment section started to become a recruitment board. It was chaotic, but sincere, and it was revealing. There were people in the comments finding prospective members the way you’d usually find a used sofa.

### The Freeloader Problem

Some of the commenters weren’t trying to join. The oldest objection, that maybe most people don’t want to take on the responsibility that anarchism requires and communal property becomes “owned by everyone, cared for by nobody,” showed up almost right away.

[an image]
The commune comments became a miniature political-philosophy seminar, as Instagram comments sometimes do.

I'd say the comment above is more true of the big socialism experiments than small communes, but I still take it seriously, because some people really would rather let somebody else take responsibility. When everybody owns everything, it can get to where nobody knows who's supposed to do what, and the same three people end up doing all the maintenance while everybody else talks about freedom. And then unofficial leaders start gaining power. Partly that's because everyone keeps handing it to them.

Communal ownership entails folks taking on visible and named stewardship duties. It requires knowing what to do if someone is leeching off the group and how to deal with it. It requires developing healthier forms of relationships. No, taking away the idea of a boss does not make everyone less passive, selfish, steal less, or stop trying to act helpless.

People want to go back to the old way of living, but they have no idea why earlier communes failed or what to do when someone wants to own land, the group runs out of money, a baby is born or someone thinks they own something. They just know they are tired and alone and want to change it.

I am not currently recruiting anyone or founding a community, which makes it easier for me to write an article like this, since I’m not trying to get you onto my land. I do plan to buy land, and people may naturally end up living around me. All of the warnings in this article apply to me, too.

[an image]
# Why Communities Keep Dying in the Same Two Ways

Most communes of my acquaintance went wrong from the inside, in one of two ways.

## The secular failure

The secular communes had a solution for how to distribute property or labor, but when the deep waters of jealousy or childhood hurt or humiliation or attraction or resentment or grief came up, the group was without a common method for dealing with it. The feelings just became agenda items.

Meeting procedure isn’t going to solve every problem, no matter how sophisticated the system of labor and money and decision making may be in a community of the [Federation of Egalitarian Communities](https://www.egalitariancommunities.org/) or any other income-sharing community. It can’t make it so that two people don’t hate each other. It can only make it so that they take turns talking about it, and that whoever raises it has to find somebody who agrees with him or her before they get to talk about it.

Eventually, when people are together long enough, politics will become a way of carrying emotional material that people can’t name. There will be a fight about a schedule or committee or noise or food or some policy or other, but it won’t be about that. There’s no shared way to talk about the hurt itself, but the meeting agenda is the one place the group lets you push for something and win, so the angry communard goes there, trying to get some justice.

## The spiritual failure

This comes about when the community realizes the importance of embracing a transformation from within, and then funnels it through a particular person, usually the founder, a teacher, a channel or some other special knower of how things really are.

[The Farm](https://thefarmcommunity.com/), in Tennessee, at its largest about 1,500 people, had many beautiful values. But in the early days, the community’s spirituality and social life followed the founder, Stephen Gaskin. From what former members have shared, the community’s doctrine ran deep into members’ intimate decisions. This is how it often goes: folks talk about oneness with the universe, while one man defines what the universe is.

The two failures mirror each other. Secular groups distribute power but leave the inner life mostly private or ignored. Spiritual groups attempt to address the inner life, but because it's the inner world being shaped by the outer as a condition of membership, we tend to find both real-world and spiritual power concentrating around whoever defines the path.

The deeper problem is that someone carries authority earned in one domain into the others. The founder who is a good teacher, the therapist who really helps people, the farmer or business manager that actually carries a lot of the economy. The danger starts when one person has the ability to define the problem, control the information related to the problem, define what the solution is, and make it hard for people to leave or express disagreement.

I dream of a way to work in depth that isn’t run by a guru, and a way of being in a community with distributed authority. A place where people who've done the healing first can join without pretending they're fully finished, and that also has peer practice and enough play that it doesn’t become a permanent repair shop.



# The Four Parts That Have to Pl/ork Together

[an image: a diagram of a house: the roof says COMMUNITY; under it the line "nothing suppressed · everything processed · authority stays with the practitioner"; three pillars: INNER PL/ORK (reparenting, somatic regulation, contemplative practice), RELATIONAL PL/ORK (peer counseling, jealousy processing, honesty practices, conflict metabolism) and MEDICINE PL/ORK (peer-guided, no shamans, gated behind the other work); the base: THE CONTAINER (membership · land · money · governance · children · exit); and below it: "Skip a domain and the community falls apart along exactly that seam." (Joel sent it on 2026-10-02 23:49: "the actual article uses an image")]
Communities tend to focus on the aspect of their project that was most interesting to the original founders, for example political types getting super into writing by-laws, or spiritual types just meditating all the time, or therapists processing each other, or people who like psychedelics discovering they’re all God together and never getting to the point of deciding who will put their name on the deed.

I’ve broken the model I propose down into four parts. Obviously the details are complicated, and jealousy, children, money, land, God, and iboga don’t fit neatly into four boxes, but let’s go with it. I’ve written detailed guides on the first three already (free to read, not a sales pitch for a retreat or anything), but this article will be mostly about the fourth.

In a nutshell, there's a difference between working together just to provide food/housing/logistics, etc., and working together to support each other in an internal practice. Why would we commit our whole lives to each other if the only thing we have is the need to take care of property? When we're all helping each other heal and be less run by fear, etc, then the hard parts mean something, and it makes sense to bind our lives together. And the outward *escuelita* and federation purpose gives us even more reason to do so, because we're not only protecting each other, but helping others build as well.

## One principle runs through all of them

Nothing suppressed, everything processed. Each of us keeps authority over our own practice, and the community is the container. Whatever answers we find stay fluid and organic, and don't freeze into doctrine.

These four parts leak into one another almost immediately. Governance can end up slyly incorporating personal tensions like jealousy. Those who have positions with more control of shared resources will automatically be affected by that psychologically (power corrupts, as they say). Those who know medicine tend to have another type of god complex since they may make life or death decisions for people routinely. How folks choose to raise children can expose values the founders never discussed. And myriad other categories arise, of course.

Also, a note on agreements: a community does need some stable agreements that they're not tweaking and revising every time somebody has a revelation in breathwork. But these agreements need to stay open to lived experience.

When agreements get frozen, religious communities tend to call the frozen version doctrine. Secular communities on the other hand often call it “the process,” which can become just as sacred.

### 1. Inner pl/ork

Pl/ork means play + work. Calling therapy “inner work” forgets the inner child, who also wants to play.

Forgive the neologism. I hope *pl/ork* isn’t too corny. 🌽

Here’s an example: you teach your inner child geography, while s/he teaches you the world is a cat!

[an image]
[Inner-child reparenting](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/inner-child-self-love-tips-and-guided) means learning to identify as the best inner adult, which is comprised of the three inner adult roles: Nurturer, Protector, and Guide. The newly developed adult reparents their newly recognized inner child. The child receives all that love, protection, and guidance that you give it, and in this process actually gains more freedom to remain alive inside you.

And it's built on [somatic regulation](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/somatic-modalities-strategic-sequencing) first. Listening to the body's feelings before making a decision with the mind. And that actually symbolizes the adult/child relationship to me in some way as well.

My contemplative practice is grounded in the early [Buddhist suttas](https://suttacentral.net/), with a critical reading. Most are treasure, while some are obviously late additions (sometimes to the point of real absurdity). A living community should relate to its own teachings in that same critical manner while staying devoted to following what they've decided on so far.

### 2. Relational pl/ork

[Hearthwork](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/hearthwork-an-integrated-peer-counseling) distributes counseling among peers: equal time, attention without interpretation or fixing, and then you switch.

The idea is that the capacity to be there for people when they need help isn’t located in one professional or guru, or the founder of the group that everyone emotionally depends on, but in the community as a whole.

Another thing is that the person listening to you shouldn’t get power, just from that, over whether or not you can be a member of the group, whether or not you can work for the group, whether or not you can live there, what happens with your children, whether or not you can take part in the medicine work, whether or not you’re believed in a dispute, etc. Letting someone turn what they learned while caring for you into administrative power over you is just creating a new hierarchy.

Another thing is knowing which problems are beyond what peers can handle and need outside or expert help.

And another is to deal with jealousy and conflict while it's still between the people involved, before it gets put on the agenda (generally at the bottom of the agenda).

Also, read my [Romance Guide](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/p/romance-advice-i-wish-my-parents), because no matter how much your founding document says that you’re all beyond romance, you’re still gonna have dyads.

### 3. Medicine pl/ork

Doing serious plant medicines carefully with peer guidance without exalting any one person as a special shaman.

This doesn’t mean that a peer-led ceremony should be done without structure. Things like screening participants, making sure the sitters are sober, having a plan for dealing with emergencies, planning for integration, and other rules and boundaries need to be dealt with beforehand. While there may be some pure learning that could come from having several altered members figure out what rules and boundaries are needed on the spot, it’s not something I recommend.

### 4. The container

Membership, land, resources, governance, children, leaving, etc.

Personally, I’m aiming for communities with less and less money involved. I think the path there has three stages.

First there will be no money exchanged between members for basic community functions like food, housing, care, tools, education, transport etc. Members might have outside jobs, and they bring an agreed share of that income in. This is probably a good place to start if someone wants to create a community now and have it be realistic.

Later, all wages and other income earned by the members from work outside the community, or from business inside the community, will be paid into the common purse of the community. No member accumulates private wealth while a member of the community. Some version of this is how things have been done in the [Bruderhof](https://www.bruderhof.com/intentional-community) community for generations, and my father lived there for 17 years. It is also done, in a somewhat different way, at [Twin Oaks](https://www.twinoaks.org/about-twinoaks-community/about-income-sharing), and a number of other income-sharing communities. So a common purse isn’t just a theory.

Eventually, the community would also stop using money outside. People would meet their needs directly, or through exchange (be it trade, gift, work, obligation, or whatever). I couldn't find a well-documented modern community that has gone this far, and in fact, it may be impractical in some locations because of government requirements like taxes on land. So perhaps the practical end point here is a community that is nearly entirely moneyless, but has a small collective cash boundary on the outside.

None of this does away with scarcity or economic power. There are lots of areas where such power can be wielded: access to food storage, housing, tools, land, medicine, transportation, and the outside world’s currency, to name a few. Even in a moneyless community, someone can control what's scarce. Who decides how these things are distributed? What do members owe one another? What happens when someone wants to leave?

These are less exciting topics to discuss spiritually. It's rare to see someone come back from an ecstatic vision with news of how to revamp the community’s policies on provisional members, or how to divvy up assets with a departing member, or how to prevent one founder from having control over the land, or what to do when a child reports something serious. And if they do, it's still something that needs a sober thinking-through.

But no amount of gorgeous land will make up for the mess that is created when one person owns the land or has the final say about what will happen on it. And when members come on board faster than the group can support them, all the peer counseling in the world won't make up for it, any more than medicine makes up for the lack of a written exit agreement.

The first three parts are the inside of the container, and this part is the container itself.

If one of them gets skipped, it will need to be dealt with eventually, at high stress, usually after the group has invested land, labor, or other resources and everyone has an opinion on how things should be.

# The Medicine Part, Without Pretending It Isn’t There

Psychedelics have moved from taboo toward regulated use much faster than most community literature has acknowledged. [Oregon’s licensed psilocybin service centers](https://www.oregon.gov/oha/ph/preventionwellness/pages/oregon-psilocybin-services.aspx) began opening in 2023. Colorado created a regulated natural-medicine system and began licensing in 2025. New Mexico enacted a [Medical Psilocybin Act](https://www.nmlegis.gov/Legislation/Legislation?Chamber=S&LegNo=219&LegType=B&year=25) in 2025. In Australia, [authorized psychiatrists have had limited access to psilocybin and MDMA](https://www.tga.gov.au/resources/explore-topic/mdma-and-psilocybine-hub) for specified conditions since 2023.

The movement is neither smooth nor inevitable. In 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued a [Complete Response Letter](https://download.open.fda.gov/crl/CRL_NDA215455_20240808.pdf) declining to approve the submitted MDMA-assisted therapy application and asking for further evidence. Portugal is often described lazily as having “legalized everything”; it actually [decriminalized possession of small amounts for personal use](https://www.euda.europa.eu/system/files/publications/642/PolicyProfile_Portugal_WEB_Final_289201.pdf) while trafficking remains criminal.

Communities therefore face real legal differences by country, state, substance, religious status, and activity. Anyone building around medicine needs actual local legal advice, not a friend who once read a thread.

Most intentional communities that use psychedelics still avoid saying so publicly. Even where the law permits some use, parents may worry about children, neighbors may imagine chaos, insurers may disappear, and a local official may understand none of the distinctions.

I’m discussing it because leaving medicine out would falsify my model. Many readers already know my [psychedelic writing](https://ibogaqueen.substack.com/s/psychedelics), including my [loveyhuasca/Haoma material](https://soma.u-dont-exist.com/). The honest version of this article has to address both the value and the risk.

The case against building medicine into community is serious. The [Global Ayahuasca Survey](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36962494/) found physical and mental adverse effects were common, although severe outcomes were much less common and context mattered. These medicines can open material faster than a person or group can support it.

They also attract people who love revelation and hate follow-through. A person can collect twelve ceremonies, six origin stories, and a new sacred name while remaining unable to apologize to a housemate. Any community organized mainly around the peak experience will eventually discover that insight does not wash dishes, revise agreements, or calm a frightened child.

The case for communal use is also real in my experience. Psychedelics can loosen defenses that otherwise dominate every serious conversation. They can create powerful bonds when people sit through difficult nights together. They can also produce confusion, grandiosity, dependency, and interpersonal mess. The question is whether the surrounding community has enough maturity to tell those apart.

## Community Is What Makes Psychedelics Pl/ork Best!

Insights need somewhere to land. You see your life with startling clarity one night and return to the same environment, where nobody knows what happened and every old cue is waiting. In community, the people who held you through the experience can also notice what happens during the following months.

Depth can increase alienation. After my original ayahuasca ego deaths at 26, I had trouble finding anyone in the physical world who seemed to have experienced anything similar. I couldn’t even find them at Buddhist monasteries despite all the preaching about enlightenment. That helped produce a God complex, a Savior complex, or both—and then attracted exactly the right people to demonstrate my limits. 😂

Trusted support is different from purchased support. The commercial alternative is often paying strangers for one night of care. Sometimes those strangers are excellent. Sometimes the person with the feather has known you for four hours and already has a cosmology for everything you say.

In community, a sober sitter may be somebody who has known you for years. Being watched and being held feel different. This matters especially with long, medically risky experiences such as iboga, where screening and continuous observation are essential.

Peers can also reality-check the downloads. Psychedelics produce genuine insight and convincing nonsense with identical lighting. Friends who know your history may notice which parts resemble a new understanding and which parts resemble your mother.

Community creates rhythm. Many traditional medicine systems place ceremonies inside communal timing rather than individual appetite. A shared calendar can reduce compulsive repetition and give integration time to happen.

The logistics become easier. Trusted childcare can be arranged collectively. People don’t need to drive away from the ceremony. Somebody can bring water, stay nearby, or sit quietly while a person returns to ordinary consciousness.

There are people to play with. Raves often create sudden intimacy among strangers before trust exists. In community, ecstatic music and movement can happen among people who already know one another’s names, histories, and inconvenient habits. 💃🕺

I won’t idealize psychedelics. Some people should avoid them, some communities shouldn’t use them, and enthusiasm will create casualties wherever competence lags behind access. A community choosing this path needs enough humility to say no, pause, refer out, and admit when an experience caused harm.

## My Ceremony Principles

No special shamans. Traditional lineages usually disagree with me here. Many ayahuasca and Bwiti communities believe medicine should remain under trained lineage authority. I respect what those traditions have preserved and have learned from them.

My objection is to placing one charismatic person above everyone else’s direct experience. A retreat-circuit facilitator may be wise, or may be unvetted, unaccountable, sexually predatory, financially dependent on repeat customers, or simply wrong. Deep openness magnifies the cost of that uncertainty.

I don’t yet know how a peer-led medicine culture prevents an informal shaman from emerging anyway—the person everybody consults, trusts, and gradually stops questioning even though nobody gave them the title. Rotating roles and public accountability may help. I don’t think either solves it completely.

I want people to learn self-guidance and reciprocal care while respecting the limits of their competence. I’ve written more about [peer-held ceremonies](http://ceremonies.u-dont-exist.com/) and about [the best psychopath shaman I ever met](http://sidney.u-dont-exist.com/).

Peer-led never means casual. Screen for medical and psychiatric contraindications. Review medications and combinations. Keep an appropriate sober sitter. Decide what requires professional or emergency care before anybody takes anything. Distributed authority raises the competence requirement; it doesn’t lower it.

I’m especially cautious about medicines and protocols I consider more destabilizing or medically burdensome, including some uses of [ketamine and MDMA](http://mdmaket.u-dont-exist.com/) and [bufo](http://bufo.u-dont-exist.com/). Those judgments are explained in the linked articles rather than smuggled into one sentence here.

The medicine stays behind the other pl/ork. Reparenting, somatic capacity, and peer counseling come first. Medicine can deepen a practice that exists. It cannot create months of honest relationship by pharmacological decree.

This prerequisite also filters out experience collectors. Somebody unwilling to spend six months learning to listen without fixing is unlikely to become more relationally mature because the visions were especially geometric.

Integration is ordinary life. Ceremony opens something. The following weeks reveal whether anything changed—in relationships, daily behavior, sleep, decisions, and the person’s ability to tolerate frustration without declaring a new spiritual emergency.

Supports matter. Preparation, nutrition, interaction screening, dose discipline, and emergency planning matter more than aesthetic ceremony details. I keep my current safety material in [Altered States Triage](https://badtrips.u-dont-exist.com/).

Legality needs a written answer. The law varies widely and sometimes ambiguously. A community should document what activities are allowed, prohibited, private, insured, or legally reviewed. “Nobody around here has heard of it” is information, not a legal opinion.

## After the Psychedelic Calling

[an image]
Many people come out of deep psychedelic or mystical experience with the same urge: find the tribe, build the village, and help other people reach whatever just opened.

I know that call. I also know the inflation that can ride beside it. You return believing love can heal anyone. Then you meet people who don’t want to change, people who sincerely want to change but keep choosing the opposite, and people whose crisis exceeds anything your enthusiasm can hold.

The call may be real. Omnipotence is a terrible founding document.

A group formed during collective spiritual euphoria can recruit too quickly, promise too much, and discover arithmetic only after several people are already dependent on it. The capacity and membership sections later in this article exist partly to protect the original generosity from that first rush.

Once the call sobers up, it can become useful. A community can serve as a training ground where people learn the practices, care for one another, and sometimes leave to begin another experiment. That answers the reasonable objection that communes are merely privileged escape pods.

## Owner rulings on rewriting Joel's own words (Joel, 2026-09-30)

These came from community sections 1 and 2 and apply to every rewrite of his words, whether by Emulate, a writer or a fix:
- **Don't hype.** "Happy" doesn't become "very happy", and "this mostly meant boredom" doesn't become "boring as hell".
- **Don't flatten a mixed experience into one note.** His childhood visits meant boredom "with some adventures mixed in".
- **Don't change a fact without asking, even a small one** ("own" to "live on").
- **Don't turn his uncertainty into a stance.** "I couldn't tell whether…" doesn't become "I didn't feel like it was really…", even when a nearby line leans that way.
- **Don't give him a reaction he couldn't have had.** He was too young to find the missing therapy practice "odd".
- **Keep the exact relation.** "Needed" isn't "wanted". "Much larger" is a comparison, and "big" drops it.
- **A fact in an AI-drafted original can be wrong.** When Joel corrects one (the "complicated labor credit system"), his correction replaces it.
- **Show every proposed change side by side before asking** (`tools/humanization/render_in_context.py`). On 2026-09-30 he approved two changes from a list, then took them back once he saw them in place.
- **Every paragraph passes alone (Joel, 2026-10-01).** A section that passes with a paragraph that fails alone doesn't count, for a published article too: "otherwise we're sort of playing with pangram but usually there are still ai tells you're missing in the paragraph, and pangram 5 will catch with better localization i'm sure." His one exception is a paragraph that really looks human to him: he has "never seen any actual human paragraph labeled as AI by pangram unless it was written as an academic paper super formulaic". A paragraph under 50 words is checked with a neighbor that passes alone.
- **Wording can flex when the meaning stays (Joel, 2026-10-01).** The preservation units are meaning, not wording.
- **A question about a passage shows the passage (Joel, 2026-10-01).** Twice he had to go and find what a question was about: "you didn't give me the context, let me go check" and "you didn't give me the block to look at". Quote the passage in the question, or put the question on the side-by-side page beside it. Say what a proposal would do to the paragraph in plain words: "anchor each point in a section 1 community" read to him as moving the points to other sections.
- **Don't ask what the rules already decide.** "Can the wording flex if the meaning stays?" got "that's already in the humanization guidelines, right?" Check the gate first, and ask only about the case it leaves open.
- **Keep his exact characters (Joel, 2026-10-02).** His own paragraphs go in with the characters he typed: straight or curly apostrophes and quotes, dashes, spacing. His section 3 P9 read 100% Human with his straight apostrophes ("who've", "they're") and 100% AI with the same words curled; my normalizing them was the only difference. His P7 passed both ways, so it isn't every paragraph, but nothing is gained by changing them. The ledger checks this with `must_contain_exact` (`tools/humanization/check_owner_edits.py`), which leaves quotes and apostrophes as they are.
- **A rewrite keeps the article's stance, checked against the whole article (Joel, 2026-10-02 00:52).** "Emulate changed 'without pretending that people arrive emotionally finished' into 'where people don't come in pre-healed' which is nearly the opposite of what i want. I DO want people to come in largely pre-healed, which is why I talk about that in the article. ... Did the reviewers not look at the article?" They hadn't, in the way that mattered: the blind trace compared each paragraph only with its own published version (it marked the change as a shift, and I let it through); the cold read saw only the section; the grounding reviewer had the whole article and missed it; and the stance ledger in step 1 had been skipped. So step 1's ledger is written before drafting, and every candidate gets the whole-article stance check before any Pangram call (step 4).
- **"I want" as an opener for his opinion (Joel, 2026-10-02).** "'I want' is generally banned as a way to introduce my opinion, as it sounds very AI. But in this article it does work because we are talking about a community that I want." That is AGENTS.md's significance-staging rule and its exception (his own wish is the subject). In his own rewrite of that paragraph he still chose "I dream of".
- **A quip that carries a point keeps the point (Joel, 2026-10-01).** Not every quip needs saving: an empty one can just go. Joel, 18:19: "we don't need to always save quips, but this quip was really meaningful and important, not like something stupid like 'it still matters on Tuesday'". The 1972 line said that forming a village had stopped sounding like a hippie leftover and started sounding like a backup plan. Said plainly as "sounded like a backup plan", it lost the first half. The trace had marked the drop, and I called it allowed. Joel put it back: "Suddenly, forming a village sounded like a good backup plan, not just a hippie utopian whim." So before cutting a quip, say what it claims; if the article needs that claim, the plain version carries all of it, both sides of a contrast included.

- **A vaguer version is rejected, not offered (Joel, 2026-10-02 21:16).** His section 4 P5 gave four specific crossings (jealousy into governance, control of resources into psychology, medicine into status, child-rearing exposing undiscussed values). Emulate's version said how people deal with jealousy is "intertwined with" running the community, the common things, parenting and medicine: everything tied to jealousy, nothing paired. I offered it as the version that passed, losing only the four directions, and recommended it. Joel: "Emulate started implying that jealousy intertwines with everything rather than each thing intertwining specifically with something. Your review should have caught that rather than simply the loss of the meaning which was bad enough, but this vagueness has to be rejected." So when specific pairings become a general tangle, the claims have changed, not just thinned: the trace marks it SHIFTED, and the version goes back for a rewrite instead of to Joel as an option. His own rewrite kept every pairing, one to a sentence, and passed.
- **The published text can be wrong about the world, and the stance check can't know it (2026-10-02).** The whole-article stance check holds a rewrite to the published essay, so it flags Joel's corrections too. In section 4 he rewrote "nobody has ever returned from an ecstatic vision announcing that the group needs a better provisional-membership policy": "people do come back from ecstatic visions with those kind of practical ideas, i've seen that, but they are often not quite as amazing as they sound to the experiencer." He also changed "may make it literally impossible" to "may be impractical in some locations". The check flagged both as conflicts. Its findings on his own paragraphs go to him as information, with my opinion on any that touch another section (for instance a child's serious report, where section 8 says the response is decided beforehand); they aren't fixes to make.
- **A quip that AI has colonized may not survive any wording (Joel, 2026-10-02 21:16).** Section 4 P7's "which can become equally sacred—just with longer meetings and fewer robes": "I was able to retain the sacred part, but no matter how i worded fewer robes and longer meetings it got flagged as AI, which yeah, it does look ai after ai colonized it." He kept the point ("which can become just as sacred") and let the quip go. "that's sad that now humans can't write in a highly polished smart way even sometimes without seeming to be ai."

## Owner bans (Joel, 2026-09-28 19:51)

These go into every writer and reviewer prompt (`tools/humanization/reviewer/owner_bans.txt`), and the linter fails the first two (O1, O2).
- "doesn't get to decide" and its family (a feeling or thing that "doesn't get to", "gets to", "gets a vote"). Joel: "one of the phrases AI completely colonized", "an optimal efficiency quippy formulation which humans just rarely use for non-humans". It came into the Make the Protector Visible drafts from my own brief.
- "Fine," "Good," "Great," as a clause of their own ("Fine, they're nice boots."). Joel: "super AI", and he had said it before.
- Wry humor. Joel: "wry in a strange way which i can't pin down". His is goofy and glad.
- Chat acronyms (IMO, TBH and the like) where the article doesn't already use them, unless the author asked for an informal internet style. Joel, 2026-10-01: "i'm surprised how many ppl i talk to don't know what IMO means", and at 18:19: "for articles where the acronyms are used, you'd use those, but for other articles where they aren't used, you wouldn't put them in unless the user asks for informal internet slang style". A writer's "IMO" went to him as a question instead of being fixed; the linter now flags one the source doesn't use.
- Abstract concepts or feelings as agents: one of the top tells to consider, not a ban. Joel, 2026-10-02 21:16: "it's actually kind of a good way to write, like you often see that used by better writers, but it can be on a range of likelihood to hear in a conversation. i don't want to straight up ban it because it's rhetorically quite nice many times, but it should be one of the top ai tells to consider, especially when it's looking super high polished or overused." His ratings of ten lines (2026-10-02 23:49; `tools/humanization/calibration/ABSTRACT-AGENTS-RATINGS-20261002.md`) matched my guesses on eight; he rated "The vision can't determine a departing member's share" more AI than I had (4 of 5), and "Hope kept that commune going for three more winters" more human (2 of 5). So an abstract agent doing an abstract job in a general claim is the strong form of the tell; one inside a small, concrete story is the weak form. Earlier, 00:52: "the usage of abstract concepts or feelings as agents is one AI tell because it permits high efficiency of words." A rewrite of his section 3 P4 said "so the anger goes there, trying to get some justice", and his minimal fix gave the action back to a person: "so the angry communard goes there, trying to get some justice". He left "politics will become a way of carrying emotional material" in the same paragraph, so fix the clear cases (a feeling or idea going somewhere, trying, wanting, deciding, refusing, arriving) with as few words changed as possible, and leave an everyday idiom ("money won't fix it") or his own words alone. The linter flags the clear cases (REVIEW, O6).
- Too many made-up scenes: a caution, not a ban. Joel, 20:13: "i'm not saying to ban made-up scenes, they can be useful, but you're overusing them here". Carry the guide's own examples first.
- Over-explaining listicles. Lists themselves are fine: "I have human and humanized paras with instructions and lists that DO pass". His way with a list is in Borrow One Competency's first paragraph (each item its own sentence, "Perhaps… Perhaps… Maybe… Even…", ending on the oddest one).
- Show every draft in context, next to the guide's original (Joel: "from now on, you need to show me your work in context"). `tools/humanization/render_in_context.py` makes that page (step 9).
